summary: Sonora sits at roughly 1,800 feet in the western Sierra Nevada foothills, which means you get genuine seasons — warm, dry summers averaging 71°F highs with abundant sunshine, and winters cold enough for frost but rarely brutal — without the snow-management headaches of towns a few thousand feet higher. The city occupies just 3.2 square miles, and its compact historic downtown along Washington Street gives it a walkable core that belies a population of only about 5,000; this is the county seat of Tuolumne County and the commercial hub for a wide rural catchment, so it punches well above its weight in services, restaurants, and small retail. Employment leans heavily on healthcare — Adventist Health Sonora is the area's largest employer — plus county government and education, which means job-switching without a major commute is possible but the pool is narrow. A home-price-to-income ratio around 6:1 is steep for a Gold Rush–era mountain town, yet median rent at $1,164 remains notably lower than most of California, creating a split where renting is manageable but buying requires stretching. The 20% poverty rate and high larceny numbers (2,251 per 100K) suggest an economy with real gaps between the service-sector floor and the professional ceiling. Yosemite's western entrance is about an hour east, and the surrounding terrain — oak-studded rolling hills dropping into river canyons — offers evening-walk scenery that flat valley towns simply can't match. Sonora is essentially a small city doing county-capital duty in wild country, which gives it both more infrastructure and more economic pressure than its size would predict.
